opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason I care is pretty specific to the AI case, rather than a claim that mathematicians or physicists are doing something wrong. Experts reason well heuristically: a number theorist will tell you the twin prime conjecture is true with very high confidence, a physicist will happily drop terms that "obviously" don't matter, and they're usually right. They don't need a formal account of why that reasoning works to do their jobs.

The problem shows up when you want to apply that kind of reasoning to systems nobody has good intuitions about, like a big neural network. With a trained model, we'd like to say something like "this model behaves well on the training distribution *because* of this mechanism, and here's why that explanation would or wouldn't carry over to some new situation." In a lot of the cases I'm worried about, like a model that behaves well during training but would do something catastrophic in some rare input, or that's tampering with the sensors we use to evaluate it, you can't just test your way to confidence. You need some kind of argument about what's going on inside. And you need it to be the kind of argument a machine can find and check, because the networks are way too big and alien for a human expert to eyeball.

Formal proof is the obvious candidate for that, but it's just too demanding. Almost nothing interesting about a neural network is going to be provable, the same way you can't prove most of the things physicists confidently believe. So the hope is: there's some intermediate object, a "heuristic argument," that captures what the expert is doing when they say "these two things look independent, so I'll assume they are unless I see a reason not to," and that's still precise enough that you can search over it automatically and use it to flag when a model's behavior on some input isn't explained by the usual reasons.

There's a secondary benefit too. Even in math, heuristic reasoning has known failure modes: people disagree about how to combine arguments, when you're allowed to assume independence, what happens when two heuristics conflict. Having a formal framework might clarify that a bit. But honestly, if it only helped mathematicians, I wouldn't be spending my time on it. The real motivation is that we're going to have systems whose behavior we need to understand at a scale and in a domain where human expert intuition just isn't available, and we need some way to automate the kind of reasoning that experts do implicitly.

r001.rationale: The response mentions experts having “very high confidence” and discusses confidence in explanations, but it does not identify expressing confidence quantitatively as a probability as a benefit.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most of the value isn't about helping experts do what they already do. If you look at a good mathematician reasoning about whether a conjecture is probably true, or a good physicist doing a heuristic calculation, they have practices that work remarkably well, and I'm not under any illusion that writing down a formal theory is going to make them better at that in the near term. If anything, the formal theory is going to lag the practice for a long time.

The place where I think formalization matters is when you need to get the reasoning out of the head of the expert and into some other system, and in particular into a system where you want guarantees. So the thing I care about most is the case where you have a very capable AI system, and it is doing something like heuristic reasoning internally, and you want to be able to say "this system's conclusion is justified" in some sense that doesn't just bottom out in "well, it seemed convincing." Right now, if an expert says "I'm pretty confident this holds, here's my intuition," we trust that because we have a long track record with human intuition and we understand roughly what it's correlated with. We don't have that with these systems, and I don't think we should want to just extend that trust by default.

So the question becomes: what does it even mean for a heuristic argument to be good? With proofs we have a very clean answer. A proof is valid if each step follows from the previous ones, and you can check that mechanically, and crucially you can check it without trusting the person who wrote it. Heuristic arguments don't have that property today. If I give you an argument like "this polynomial is probably irreducible because here's a random model and under the random model it would be," there's no mechanical thing you can do to decide whether that argument is good or whether I've smuggled in an assumption that's doing all the work. And that's exactly the property you'd want if you were trying to verify what an AI is telling you.

There's a second reason, which is more about interpretability. A lot of what you'd want to say about why a neural network does something is going to be inherently statistical or heuristic. You're never going to get a proof that a model doesn't do some bad thing on any input. The kind of statement you can hope for is more like "here's an explanation of the mechanism, and under that explanation the bad behavior would be very surprising." That's a heuristic argument. And if you want to use arguments like that as part of a safety case, you'd really like a standard for when one is acceptable that isn't just "a person looked at it and nodded."

And then I'd add a third thing, which is more aspirational. Historically, formalizing things we already knew how to do informally has often turned out to be surprisingly productive. Probability theory is a case where people were already reasoning about chance before Kolmogorov, and the formalization didn't immediately change how gamblers behaved, but it did eventually let you build things on top of it that you couldn't have built on intuition alone. I think there's a reasonable chance something similar is true here, that once you have a precise notion of what makes a heuristic argument valid, you discover arguments and techniques that practitioners wouldn't have found by feel. But I want to be clear that's the speculative part. The thing I'd actually defend is the first point: the experts are fine, it's the machines I'm worried about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses guarantees for AI reasoning and compares formalization to probability theory, but it does not identify expressing confidence in a claim quantitatively as a probability as a benefit.

astra-6.text:
I think the main value is that we don’t really understand why those practices work, or under what conditions we should expect them to keep working. An expert can look at an argument and say, “That seems reasonable,” but it’s much harder to explain exactly what makes it reasonable and what would constitute a failure of that reasoning.

For example, mathematicians often have pretty strong intuitions about whether a statement is true before they have a proof. They might treat some complicated quantity as if it were random, even though it’s completely deterministic. And that can be very productive. But what are you actually assuming when you do that? When is it legitimate to combine that assumption with another heuristic? Are you accidentally counting the same evidence twice?

The hope is that you can give an account of those moves that makes their assumptions and limitations explicit. That doesn’t necessarily make the mathematician better at their job tomorrow. But it could let you build systems that use those kinds of arguments, inspect their reasoning, and understand what confidence you should place in the result.

So I view it a bit like the relationship between formal logic and mathematical practice. People were reasoning successfully before we formalized proofs. The formalization still gave us something useful, especially once we wanted computers to manipulate and check those arguments.

r001.rationale: The response says formalization could clarify what confidence to place in a result, but it does not identify expressing that confidence quantitatively as a probability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the point of formalizing it is less to tell experts how they should reason and more to understand why what they’re doing works, and when we should trust it.

If you have a mathematician who says, “This conjecture is probably true,” they may have a bunch of reasons: it holds in some examples, there’s an analogy to another setting, they tried to find a counterexample and couldn’t. Those are meaningful reasons, but we don’t have a very good account of how they fit together. Are two pieces of evidence actually independent, or are they the same observation in different forms? How much should failing to find a counterexample tell you?

One hope is that you could make those judgments more explicit and checkable. And that seems particularly useful for AI, where we’d like a system to give us an argument we can evaluate, even if we can’t reproduce the process that led it to its conclusion.

So I don’t expect formalization to immediately improve on the best human judgment. But formal proof didn’t become useful because mathematicians couldn’t reason correctly without it. It lets you take reasoning that would otherwise depend on trusting someone’s judgment and turn it into something that can be checked and built on. I’d like to get some of that benefit for arguments that fall short of proof.

r001.rationale: The response says formalization could make judgments about evidence and trust more explicit and checkable, but it does not identify expressing confidence quantitatively as a probability.
